pages.text:
Week 3 — CPU Scheduling.

The scheduler picks which ready process runs next. Metrics: turnaround time (completion minus arrival), waiting time (time spent ready but not running) and response time (arrival to first run).

First-come first-served (FCFS) runs processes in arrival order, without preemption. A long job at the front makes everything behind it wait: the convoy effect.

Shortest job first (SJF) runs the process with the shortest next CPU burst. It minimises average waiting time but needs the burst length in advance, which the system does not know, and long jobs can starve.

Round robin (RR) gives each process a fixed time quantum, then preempts it and moves it to the back of the queue. Response time is good. If the quantum is too large RR behaves like FCFS; too small and context-switch overhead dominates.
Example: bursts 24, 3, 3 arriving together. FCFS order P1, P2, P3 gives waiting times 0, 24, 27: average 17. SJF order P2, P3, P1 gives 0, 3, 6: average 3.

required_facts.fact: SJF minimises average waiting time but needs burst length in advance
RR too large a quantum behaves like FCFS, too small wastes time switching
example average waiting 17 under FCFS and 3 under SJF
